title: Corpay's Agent Card Solves the Credential Problem. It Doesn't Solve the Authorization Problem.
brief: Virtual cards give AI agents a payment instrument. They don't answer who is legally liable when an agent pays without explicit human consent.

title: The Agentic Payments Alliance Is Writing De Facto Law. That's the Problem.
brief: When Visa, Mastercard, and Circle write agent commerce standards together, certification scope and competitive advantage are the same decision.

title: MPP, Agent Pay, and AP2 Each Solve Delegation. None Solve the Authorization Logic That Comes After.
brief: Three protocols are racing to authenticate AI agents in payments. The gap isn't authentication — it's that no spec defines what an agent is allowed to decide, and when.

title: The Real Agentic Payments Battle Is Over the Decision Loop, Not the Rails
brief: Visa, Mastercard, and Google each solved a different layer of agentic payments. The missing layer is cross-network authorization metadata — and no scheme standard carries it yet.

title: Agentic Payments Break the Liability Stack Before Regulators Finish Reading the Docket
brief: SCA and tokenization solve single-session fraud. Multi-agent procurement chains create liability gaps no chargeback right, AML flag, or SCA exemption was designed to close.

title: Mastercard Built the Rails for Agent Payments. Nobody Built the Law.
brief: Mastercard Agent Pay tokenizes AI-initiated transactions. But authorization law still requires a human to have consented — and agents aren't humans.

title: Agentic Payments Have a Fraud Stack Problem That Credentials Alone Cannot Fix
brief: Visa CLI and x402 solve agent credential issuance. Neither solves the fraud detection gap where a compromised agent is behaviorally indistinguishable from a legitimate one.

title: Mastercard and Visa Are Racing to Own the Policy Layer, Not Just the Rails
brief: Agent Pay and Inflow-issued agent cards solve execution. The unsolved problem is who enforces permission limits when the human isn't watching.

title: AP2, x402, and Visa MCP Are All Solving Authorization. None of Them Solve Dispute Resolution.
brief: Three protocols launched, 60+ partners aligned, and one problem still unowned: what happens when an AI agent buys the wrong thing and nobody can prove intent.

title: AP2 Solves Agent Authorization. It Does Not Solve Agent Drift.
brief: An arXiv paper catalogues five breaks in x402, not AP2. But the deeper problem — agents acting on stale delegations — isn't a protocol flaw in either. It's a missing runtime layer that neither proposal specifies.

title: The Gap None of Them Have Solved: Runtime Scope Negotiation in Agentic Payments
brief: Visa, Mastercard, and Cloudflare have all published delegated-auth specs. None of them operate at agent runtime speed, asynchronously, mid-task. That gap is the constraint.

title: Agent Tokens Are Real. The Merchant-Side Provisioning Gap Is Why They're Not Running Your Spend Yet.
brief: Mastercard and Visa have agent-bound token architectures. The constraint isn't credential issuance — it's that merchants haven't provisioned for them.

title: AP2 Establishes Agent Credentials. A402 Proposes Agent Payment Flows. Neither Solves Conditional Clearing.
brief: AP2 establishes agent credential standards and A402 proposes HTTP-native micropayment flows — but conditional clearing at agent speed remains unaddressed by either.

title: The Missing Layer in Agentic Payments Is Session-Level Policy Enforcement, Not the Rails
brief: Issuers have velocity limits. Schemes have liability rules. Neither enforces policy across a multi-step agent session in real time. That gap is the next infrastructure problem.

title: The Permission Layer That Agentic Payments Are Missing Isn't in the Protocol — It's Between the Issuer and the Agent
brief: x402 and Stripe MPP solve different layers. Neither resolves who authorized what when an agent acts across a multi-step session.

title: Agentic Payments Have No 'Scope Exceeded' Reason Code — That's the Real Liability Gap
brief: 3DS2 and chargeback rules were built for human principals. When an agent overspends, no existing reason code fits. That's not a gap in rails — it's a gap in liability taxonomy.

title: Visa Can Verify an Agent Exists. Nobody Can Verify What the Agent Agreed To.
brief: Agent identity is now a solved layer. The missing layer is a legally valid record of what the agent was authorized to do when it transacted.

title: 165 Million x402 Transactions: What the Number Actually Counts Determines Whether the Thesis Holds
brief: x402's 165M figure could mean channel opens, HTTP 402 responses, or settlements. That definitional gap is the whole agentic payments story.

title: FIDO Can Authenticate Your Agent. It Cannot Authorize What Your Agent Decides.
brief: Authentication proves an agent is who it claims. The missing layer is authorizing what the agent is allowed to decide—and that gap is where liability lands.

title: Mastercard and PayPal Just Solved Agent Authentication. The Dispute Layer Is Still Broken.
brief: Agent Pay + PayPal checkout is a real milestone. But when an agent disputes a charge, no one has built the stack to adjudicate it.

title: Agentic Tokens Solve Authorization. They Don't Solve Who Authorized the Authorizer.
brief: Visa and Mastercard have live agentic transaction rails. The missing layer is provable delegation: who told the agent it could spend, and can you prove it after the fact?

title: Mandate Drift and Mandate Ambiguity Are Different Problems — And the Payments Stack Solves Neither
brief: Scheme-level agent controls scope spending rules but can't track when policy context changes or when the original instruction was never machine-interpretable.

title: Visa Is Building the Trust Layer for Agentic Payments — But the Moat Isn't Dug Yet

brief: Visa's agentic push is really a credential play. The question isn't whether agents need identity — it's whether interchange survives long enough to fund it.

title: The Agentic Payments Race Is Not About Rails — It's About Who Owns Compliance Architecture

title: Consumers Will Kill Agentic Payments Before Regulators Do
brief: 55% of consumers won't let agents pay autonomously. The real blocker isn't law or rails — it's consent. And nobody building the infrastructure is solving for that.

brief: x402 and UCP are both chasing the same prize: the moment an AI agent decides to pay. The infrastructure question is already settled. The governance question isn't.
